subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: lending to a friend without a plan [Pitfall]
passage:
After-school club note, Friday.
Shankar was unusually quiet at the craft table today. When I asked, he told me that three weeks ago he had lent Yusuf all his savings, one hundred and fifty rupees, for a cricket camp form. Yusuf had said, "I'll give it back next week, promise." Nothing had been said since, and on Wednesday Shankar missed the deadline for the school trip money. He said asking felt awkward, so he had kept quiet. I suggested he speak to Yusuf calmly, and I stayed nearby. Yusuf looked surprised; he had honestly forgotten, and said he would talk to his parents tonight. Afterwards Shankar said, "Next time I'll lend only a little, and we'll fix a day first." I have let both families know.
Club supervisor

qa.q: How much did Shankar lend Yusuf?
qa.a: One hundred and fifty rupees, all his savings.

qa.q: Why had Shankar kept quiet for three weeks?
qa.a: Asking for his own money back felt awkward, so he stayed silent even as the trip deadline passed, and he seemed unhappy about it.

qa.q: What else could Shankar have done before lending such a large amount?
qa.a: He could have told a parent first, so an adult could help agree a clear return date and he would not be left short.

qa.q: How did Yusuf react when Shankar spoke to him?
qa.a: Yusuf looked surprised, had honestly forgotten, and said he would talk to his parents tonight.

grounding: A club supervisor records a boy who lent his savings to a friend without a return date and missed a payment of his own.

subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: lending to a friend without a plan [Pitfall]
passage:
Sunday
Today was the last day of the book fair and I couldn't buy the space encyclopedia. Why? Because two weeks ago Lavanya said, "Lend me your two hundred, I'll return it Monday, pakka." I gave it all. Monday came. Then another Monday. Every time I opened my mouth to ask, it felt like begging for a favour, not asking for my own money. Today at the fair I finally asked. Lavanya slapped her forehead. "Oh no, I totally forgot!" She wasn't lying, I think. She said she'd bring it on Tuesday. But the fair is over. New rule for me: small amounts only, and we say the day out loud before I hand anything over.
Pranav

qa.q: What couldn't Pranav buy at the book fair?
qa.a: The space encyclopedia.

qa.q: How did asking for the money feel to Pranav?
qa.a: It felt like begging for a favour, so Pranav felt uncomfortable and kept putting it off.

qa.q: What other approach could help Pranav if Tuesday passes too?
qa.a: Pranav could ask a parent to help sort it out with Lavanya's family, since an adult can settle a stuck loan without a quarrel.

qa.q: How does Lavanya seem to experience being asked?
qa.a: Lavanya seems embarrassed, slapping her forehead, and appears to have genuinely forgotten.

grounding: A diary entry shows a child who lent savings without a clear plan, missed a book fair purchase and decided how to lend next time.

subtype: Approach: task decomposition into a packing and route list [Action]
passage:
"Maa, I've made the list for Dida and Dadu's."
"Rajni, it's a week away!" Bidisha laughed. "Let me see."
"One: tickets. Two: pack clothes. Three: food for the train. Four: a gift for Dida."
"Tickets are done. Baba booked them yesterday."
"Tick!" Rajni drew a fat tick. "Clothes I'll pack on Thursday. Two frocks, the shawl Dida likes, and my slippers."
"And the train food?"
"Luchi and aloo dum, packed the night before. Water bottles. Paper plates."
"Plates? Your Baba forgets plates every single time."
"That's why I wrote it big." Rajni underlined it twice. "Five: ask Mitali-mashi to feed Tommy."
"The dog! I forgot about the dog."
"Tick, when she says yes."

qa.q: What will Rajni pack on Thursday?
qa.a: Two frocks, the shawl Dida likes, and her slippers.

qa.q: How does Rajni seem to feel while working through the list?
qa.a: She seems proud and eager, drawing a fat tick and underlining the plates twice. 😊

qa.q: What else could make Rajni's list even more useful?
qa.a: Writing a day beside each task, so the jobs are spread through the week instead of piling up the night before.

qa.q: How does Bidisha experience the list?
qa.a: Bidisha is amused and impressed, and relieved when Rajni remembers the dog she had forgotten.

grounding: A girl breaks a visit to her grandparents into tasks and ticks them off with her mother a week ahead.

subtype: Approach: task decomposition into a packing and route list [Action]
passage: Last Diwali, when we went to see Nani and Nana in Nagpur, Mummy let me, Seema, be the list-maker. A week before, I sat at the dining table with a pad and broke the trip into jobs: tickets, clothes for four days, food for the twelve-hour train, a present for Nana, and someone to water our plants. Every evening Mummy and I went down the list together. Some jobs took one minute; my little sister Indu packed her own socks. Some took three evenings, like finding Nana's favourite tea. On the day we left, the only thing not ticked was "relax". On the train, while other families ran to buy food at stations, we opened our steel tiffins and ate slowly. I felt very grown-up.

qa.q: How long was the train journey?
qa.a: Twelve hours.

qa.q: How did Seema feel on the train?
qa.a: Seema felt proud and grown-up, eating calmly while other families rushed for food.

qa.q: Which other approach could work for a trip like this, and why?
qa.a: Starting from an old checklist of past trips would save time, but breaking this trip into its own jobs fitted what this visit needed.

qa.q: What was it like for Indu to be part of the plan?
qa.a: Indu got a small job of her own, packing her own socks, so she was included too.

grounding: Looking back, a child describes breaking a family visit into tasks and checking them off with Mummy the week before.

subtype: Approach: comparing travel options by cost and comfort [Thinking]
passage:
"Papa, I made a table for Agra," Jagdish said, sliding his notebook across.
Mohit, his father, put his phone down. "Let's hear it."
"Car: we can stop wherever we want, for dhabas and photos. But fuel and tolls cost a lot, and you'd drive half the night. You get sleepy, Papa."
"True."
"Bus: cheapest. But Dadi's knees hurt in bus seats for nine hours."
"Hmm. And the train?"
"Costs less than the car. We sleep in berths, there's a toilet, and nobody has to drive in the dark."
"But no stops for photos."
"We can take photos in Agra, Papa."
Mohit laughed and opened the booking page. "Sleeper or AC?"
Jagdish grinned. "Let me make another table."

qa.q: Which option did Jagdish call the cheapest?
qa.a: The bus.

qa.q: What was Jagdish worried about with the car?
qa.a: He was worried about Papa driving half the night and getting sleepy.

qa.q: What else could Jagdish have weighed besides cost?
qa.a: How each person travels best, since Dadi's knees and Papa's tiredness show that comfort differs from person to person.

qa.q: How does Mohit see Jagdish's table?
qa.a: Mohit takes it seriously, seems amused and pleased, and lets Jagdish work on the next choice too.

grounding: A boy compares car, bus and train for a family trip to Agra and talks his father into the train.

subtype: Approach: comparing travel options by cost and comfort [Thinking]
passage: When Parveen-aunty wanted to drive us all to Agra last winter, I was the one who said, "Wait." I'm Jeevan, and I like lists. I drew three columns in my maths notebook: train, bus, car. The car meant Aunty driving six hours each way, fog on the highway, but stopping for parathas whenever we liked. The bus was cheap but cramped. The train cost less than fuel and tolls together, and nobody would have to watch the road in the dark on the way back. I showed Aunty. She read it twice, then booked the train. We never got those highway parathas. But on the ride home, in the fog, I watched her sleep with her mouth open, and I felt I'd done something useful.

qa.q: How long would Aunty have driven each way?
qa.a: Six hours.

qa.q: How did Jeevan feel watching Aunty sleep on the ride home?
qa.a: Jeevan felt useful and quietly pleased that the train let Aunty rest.

qa.q: Which other approach might suit a trip with more stops?
qa.a: The car, because it allows stopping for food and sights; it could work better on a daytime trip without fog.

qa.q: What was the train choice like for Parveen-aunty?
qa.a: She could rest instead of driving in fog, though she gave up the highway parathas.

grounding: A child compares three ways to travel to Agra and helps the family choose the train for its cost and safety after dark.

subtype: Approach: making a wish list without limits [Pitfall]
passage: In the waiting room of the eye clinic, while Dadi was inside, Gurpreet unfolded a tourist map of Jaipur across his knees. "Papa, the weekend: the fort, the palace of winds, the zoo, the water palace, the wax museum and the village dinner place. Six places! Two days!" His father smiled and borrowed the map. "Look. The fort is here, the zoo is here, the dinner place is way out here." He traced the roads with a finger, then pointed at the big wall clock. "Each drive is about an hour in traffic. The fort alone takes a morning. Count." Gurpreet counted on his fingers, and his grin slipped. "That's more hours than we're awake." Nurse Manjula called Dadi's name. Gurpreet folded the map slowly and crossed out two places.

qa.q: How many places did Gurpreet want to visit in two days?
qa.a: Six places.

qa.q: What does Gurpreet's slipping grin show?
qa.a: He felt disappointed as he realised his exciting list could not fit into two days.

qa.q: What would you change first in Gurpreet's planning?
qa.a: Checking the distances and how long each stop takes before choosing, then picking only two or three places a day.

qa.q: How might Papa see the list?
qa.a: Papa takes the excitement kindly, but uses the map and clock so Gurpreet can see the problem for himself.

grounding: A boy's wish list of six places in two days falls apart once his father shows him the map and the time each drive takes.

subtype: Approach: making a wish list without limits [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Karthik, Sumit's cousin, and I was staying with them when the Ooty plan happened. Sumit had written on the fridge whiteboard: lake, tea factory, botanical garden, toy train, the peak, the falls. Under it: SATURDAY + SUNDAY. He kept tapping the board. "All six, Appa, easy." His father didn't argue. He opened the road map on the table and put his watch beside it. "Falls to the peak, see this road? It bends like a noodle. One hour. The toy train, half a day." Sumit looked from the map to the watch for a long time. Then he rubbed out the falls and the tea factory himself. He was quiet at dinner. I couldn't tell if he was sulking or just thinking.

qa.q: What was written under the six places?
qa.a: SATURDAY + SUNDAY.

qa.q: What might Sumit have been feeling as he looked from the map to the watch?
qa.a: He was probably deflated and a little embarrassed, seeing that his 'easy' plan could not fit.

qa.q: What else could Sumit try when planning next time?
qa.a: Marking each place on the map with its travel time before writing the list, so the limits show up early.

qa.q: How does Karthik read Sumit at dinner?
qa.a: Karthik notices Sumit is quiet but cannot tell whether it is sulking or thinking.

grounding: A cousin watches a boy's impossible two-day list shrink once his father sets a map and a watch in front of him.

subtype: Approach: adjusting the plan to fit the budget [Revision]
passage:
Saturday, Gwalior
We came back to the guest house tired and happy. Last week, when Mummy said we had only ten thousand rupees for the whole trip, my plan fell apart. I'd put the water park first, and Vandana-mausi found out the tickets alone were almost three thousand for all of us. So I sat with the paper again. The fort is nearly free, the museum is cheap, and the water park was really just for me. I crossed it out. Today we climbed the fort, and Nani found the old carvings she'd read about. At the museum Chotu pressed his nose to the glass in front of the swords. Nobody missed the water park. Not even me. Mostly.
Gargi

qa.q: How much did Mummy say they had for the whole trip?
qa.a: Ten thousand rupees.

qa.q: How does Gargi feel about dropping the water park?
qa.a: Gargi feels a small pang of disappointment, as 'Mostly' shows, but is mostly content because everyone enjoyed the day.

qa.q: What else could Gargi have done instead of dropping the water park completely?
qa.a: Gargi could have suggested saving it for a later trip, so the wish is postponed rather than lost.

qa.q: What was the day like for Nani?
qa.a: Nani found the old carvings she had read about, so the revised plan gave her something she cared about.

grounding: A diary entry shows a child cutting the costly water park from a trip plan to fit the family budget, and the day still going well.

subtype: Approach: adjusting the plan to fit the budget [Revision]
passage: In their small house in Dewas, Noor had drawn the Indore trip on the back of an old calendar: water park, the palace, the museum, a big dinner. Then she heard Ammi and Farida-khala counting in low voices in the kitchen. "Ten thousand, with the bus and the room. That's all." Noor looked at her calendar. The water park was four people times eight hundred, plus lockers. She sat on the doorstep and worked it out. The palace and the museum together cost less than a quarter of that. That night she handed Ammi a new plan with the water park crossed out and a line added: "Kachoris in the night market instead." Ammi hugged her. Two weeks later, walking through the palace halls, Farida-khala said it was the best day she'd had in years.

qa.q: What had Noor drawn on the back of the calendar?
qa.a: The Indore trip: water park, the palace, the museum and a big dinner.

qa.q: What made Noor rethink the plan, and how did she seem to feel?
qa.a: Hearing Ammi and Farida-khala counting in low voices, she seemed worried about the tight budget and wanted to help.

qa.q: What else could Noor have done if she still really wanted the water park?
qa.a: She could have asked whether it could replace the palace or wait for another trip, choosing openly with the family instead of quietly giving it up.

qa.q: How did Farida-khala experience the revised trip?
qa.a: Farida-khala said it was the best day she'd had in years.

grounding: A girl who overhears the trip budget removes the expensive water park and keeps the cheaper palace and museum, which everyone enjoys.

subtype: Approach: asking each family member for one wish [Action]
passage: I'm Alka, Jagdish's sister, and I thought his idea would end in a fight. On our last trip, to Mysore, Papa wanted temples, Mummy wanted silk shops, and Dadi sat in the car sulking. This time Jagdish came round with four chits. "One place each. Anything." Dadi wrote the hill temple. Mummy wrote the silk market. Papa wrote the railway museum, which surprised everyone. I wrote the zoo. Jagdish pinned the chits on the calendar, two for each day, and put his own wish, the palace lights, on Sunday night. On the trip, Dadi prayed a long time on the hill and nobody hurried her. I'm not sure what Jagdish was thinking when Papa laughed at the old engines, but he kept looking round at all of us.

qa.q: What did Papa write on his chit?
qa.a: The railway museum.

qa.q: What might Jagdish have been feeling when he kept looking round at everyone?
qa.a: He seemed quietly pleased and watchful, perhaps relieved that each person was enjoying their own pick.

qa.q: What else could the family try if two wishes clash on the same day?
qa.a: They could swap the days or take turns choosing the order, keeping the fair idea of one place each.

qa.q: How did the plan look to Dadi this time?
qa.a: Instead of sulking in the car, Dadi got to pray on the hill as long as she liked, with nobody hurrying her.

grounding: A sister watches a boy ask each family member for one place and build the trip days around those choices.

subtype: Approach: asking each family member for one wish [Action]
passage:
Sunday: Back from Madurai, everyone was cross. Ammamma had missed the temple she wanted, and Harsha's sister Diya had spent the trip in shops she hated. Harsha sat on the stairs for a long time.
Wednesday: Before the Puducherry trip, Harsha went to each person with a notebook. "Pick one place. Just one." Ammamma chose the old church by the sea, Amma the sunrise walk on the beach, his father Suraj the bakery lane, and Diya, after long thought, the botanical garden. Harsha fitted two into each day.
The next month: On the last evening in Puducherry, Diya was sketching leaves she had collected in the garden. Suraj bought everyone one more pastry, and Ammamma said, "This time everybody got a turn."

qa.q: What did Diya choose?
qa.a: The botanical garden.

qa.q: Why did Harsha sit on the stairs after Madurai, and what might he have felt?
qa.a: Everyone had come back cross, so he probably felt troubled and wanted the next trip to be fairer.

qa.q: What else could Harsha try on a longer trip?
qa.a: Asking everyone for a first and second choice, so if one place is closed there is still something each person looks forward to.

qa.q: How did the plan look to Ammamma?
qa.a: Ammamma felt everybody got a turn, unlike Madurai when she missed her temple.

grounding: Across several weeks, a boy asks each family member to choose one place and builds the trip around their wishes so nobody feels ignored.

subtype: Approach: preparing for rain and delays [Thinking]
passage: Keerthana, your Amma was always the careful one. When Vasudha was nine, we planned a trip to Mysore in the monsoon, and I said, "Rain? We'll manage." She sat with her chin on her knees and said, "Appa, the train is always late in the rain. What if we wait two hours at the station? What if it pours the day we see the palace?" Then she answered herself. "We take murukku and bananas for the waiting. We take that old plastic sheet to sit on. And we find something indoors, like the museum." I laughed at her. The train was three hours late, and the station benches were wet. We sat on her sheet eating murukku. Next day it poured, and we spent a happy afternoon in the museum.

qa.q: How late was the train?
qa.a: Three hours.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling while sitting with her chin on her knees?
qa.a: She seemed worried about a long wait and rain, then more settled once she had thought of snacks, a sheet and an indoor plan.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story turned out to matter most?
qa.a: Carrying the plastic sheet and murukku, because the late train and wet benches made them the most useful things the family had.

qa.q: How did the elder see Vasudha's idea at first?
qa.a: The elder laughed at it, sure they would manage, until the late train and the rain proved her right.

grounding: An elder recalls a girl thinking ahead about a late train and rain and suggesting snacks, a sheet and a museum as a wet-day plan.

subtype: Approach: preparing for rain and delays [Thinking]
passage: Seema's family had one hour before leaving for the station, and the sky over Kalka was already grey. Her father was hunting for the tickets; her brother Naveen was hunting for his cap. Seema stood at the window thinking. "The toy train was late last time. And if it rains in Shimla, we'll be stuck in the hotel room all afternoon." She said it out loud to Naveen, who shrugged. So she did it herself: a bag of roasted chana and biscuits in the side pocket, the folded plastic sheet from the storeroom, and on a scrap of paper, "Rain plan: the state museum." The train left forty minutes late. It drizzled. Naveen sat on her plastic sheet on the damp platform and ate half the chana.

qa.q: What did Seema write on the scrap of paper?
qa.a: "Rain plan: the state museum."

qa.q: What was Seema thinking as she stood at the window?
qa.a: She was uneasy about a late train and rain trapping them indoors, so she wanted a back-up ready.

qa.q: What else could Seema have done in that one hour?
qa.a: She could have asked her father to check the train timing and the weather, so the family planned together instead of her doing it alone.

qa.q: How does Naveen experience Seema's preparation?
qa.a: He shrugged at first, but ended up sitting on her sheet and eating half the chana. 😅

grounding: Under time pressure, a girl thinks through a late train and rain and packs snacks, a sheet and an indoor plan.

subtype: Approach: leaving the whole plan to the adults [Pitfall]
passage:
Tuesday, Hampi
Everyone's asleep and I'm writing by torchlight. Two weeks ago, when Usha-chithi asked, "Varun, what do you want to see in Hampi?" I said, "Anything," and went back to my game. Today was temples. Then more temples. Then a market with only brass lamps. I wanted the round basket-boat ride on the river that my friend told me about, but nobody knew I wanted it, so it wasn't in the plan. I sulked at lunch and Chithi asked what was wrong. I said "nothing" again. Now it's our last night. I think the only person I can be angry with is me.
Varun

qa.q: What did Varun want to do in Hampi?
qa.a: The round basket-boat ride on the river.

qa.q: How does Varun feel on the last night?
qa.a: Varun feels disappointed and a bit angry with himself for saying 'anything' when asked.

qa.q: What else could Varun have done when Usha-chithi asked two weeks ago?
qa.a: Varun could have named one thing, like the basket boats; even one wish gives the adults something to plan around.

qa.q: What might the trip have been like for Usha-chithi?
qa.a: She asked twice and still didn't know what Varun wanted, so she may have felt puzzled and a little hurt by the sulking.

grounding: A diary entry shows a child who left all the trip planning to adults and then felt unhappy that the places did not suit the child's interests.

subtype: Approach: leaving the whole plan to the adults [Pitfall]
passage: When the families on their lane in a village near Salem planned a day at the big fair in the next town, Parveen-akka, who organised everything, went to every house asking what each person wanted to see. Karthik was flying his kite. "Whatever. You decide," he called down from the roof. On the day, the list was the temple, the cloth stalls, a relative's house for lunch, and the cattle show. Karthik dragged his feet at every stop. He had wanted the giant wheel and the magic show tent, but by the time he mentioned them, the bus was leaving. On the way home he kicked the seat in front. His mother whispered, "Akka asked you, kanna." Karthik stared out of the window and said nothing.

qa.q: What was Karthik doing when Parveen-akka came round?
qa.a: He was flying his kite on the roof.

qa.q: What does Karthik kicking the seat suggest?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and let down, perhaps partly with himself for not speaking up.

qa.q: What could Karthik do before the next outing?
qa.a: Tell Parveen-akka one or two things he wants when she asks, so they can be fitted into the day.

qa.q: How might Parveen-akka see Karthik's sulking?
qa.a: She asked everyone so the day would be fair, so she may feel a little frustrated that he said 'whatever' and then was unhappy.

grounding: A boy ignores the chance to give his wishes for a family outing and ends up unhappy at places that do not interest him.

subtype: Approach: drawing a map with a timetable [Action]
passage: Tanvir, you want to plan your college trip on your phone? Let me tell you how I, Rashmi, planned my first one on paper. I was eleven, and we were going to Darjeeling for three days. My father had a list of nine places. I took a sheet from my exercise book and drew the road from Siliguri up the hills, with little boxes for each day: morning, afternoon, evening. Then I asked the hotel manager how long each drive took, and wrote it in red between the boxes. Sunrise point, the zoo, the tea garden, the monastery, the toy train... Day one's boxes were overflowing with red. I moved two places to day three. My father looked at my map and said, "Beti, you've saved us from crying in a jeep."

qa.q: How many days was the Darjeeling trip?
qa.a: Three days.

qa.q: What might young Rashmi have felt when day one's boxes overflowed with red?
qa.a: Probably a jolt of worry, then relief at catching the problem on paper before the trip.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story made the plan work?
qa.a: Asking how long each drive took and writing it between the boxes, because that showed day one was far too full.

qa.q: How did Rashmi's father see the map?
qa.a: Rashmi's father was relieved and grateful, joking that the map saved them from crying in a jeep.

grounding: An elder recalls sketching a trip route with morning, afternoon and evening boxes to check whether the timings were realistic.

subtype: Approach: drawing a map with a timetable [Action]
passage: Their connecting train left Chennai at seven in the evening, and Amma's phone had died on the overnight journey. Uma borrowed a paper napkin from the station canteen and a pen from her cousin Disha. "The beach, the museum, the aquarium, and Disha-akka's favourite dosa place," she said, drawing a wobbly line between four circles. Under the line she made three boxes: morning, afternoon, evening. Then she asked the man at the enquiry counter how long an auto took between each. Beach to museum, twenty minutes. Museum to the aquarium, nearly an hour in traffic. "The aquarium is too far," Uma said, crossing it out. At six, full of dosa, they were back on the platform with an hour to spare.

qa.q: When did the connecting train leave?
qa.a: At seven in the evening.

qa.q: How might Uma have felt when she crossed out the aquarium?
qa.a: She may have felt a little disappointed, but also sensible and in control, keeping the family safe for the train.

qa.q: What else could Uma have tried if she had no paper at all?
qa.a: She could have asked the enquiry counter which two places were closest to the station and kept the day to those.

qa.q: What was the day like for Disha?
qa.a: Disha got to eat at the dosa place she loved without worrying about missing the train.

grounding: With a dead phone and a fixed train time, a girl sketches a route with time boxes to check which stops are realistic.

subtype: Approach: packing checklist based on past trips [Thinking]
passage: Dolma, bring that old notebook from the shelf. See the first page? I wrote this when I was a boy of ten. The year before, we had gone to Rishikesh, and on the second night my mother's headache came and nobody had packed her tablets. Then my father's charger turned out to be still plugged in at home, so we couldn't call my aunt to say we had arrived. Two small things, and the whole trip felt spoiled. So the next year, before anything else, I wrote at the top: 1. Amma's medicine. 2. Charger. Only after that: clothes, towels, snacks. I made my mother check number one. Every trip since, the list has started the same way. Even now, I, Ramesh, pack those two first.

qa.q: What were the first two items on the list?
qa.a: Amma's medicine and the charger.

qa.q: How did young Ramesh feel about the Rishikesh trip?
qa.a: He felt the whole trip was spoiled, frustrated that two small forgotten things caused so much trouble.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story mattered most?
qa.a: Writing the forgotten items at the top before anything else, so last year's mistakes could not happen again.

qa.q: How might Ramesh's mother have been affected by the list?
qa.a: On the Rishikesh trip she had a headache with no tablets; with her medicine as number one, she could travel without that worry.

grounding: An elder recalls writing a packing list that begins with the medicine and charger forgotten on an earlier trip.

subtype: Approach: packing checklist based on past trips [Thinking]
passage: The lights went out at nine, and the taxi was coming at five in the morning. Vaibhav's parents were packing by torchlight, sighing. Vaibhav sat on the bed with a notebook and a candle. "Last time at Nani's," he said, "Gurleen got a fever and we had no medicine, and Papa's charger was still in the wall here." He wrote MEDICINE BOX in big letters at the top, then CHARGER, and drew a box beside each. Then clothes, toothbrushes, snacks. When Mummy tried to zip the big bag, he stopped her. "Box one, box two, first." She found the medicine box on the fridge and the charger by the television, and he ticked both. Gurleen, half asleep, asked if she could tick the snacks.

qa.q: When was the taxi coming?
qa.a: At five in the morning.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav stop Mummy from zipping the bag?
qa.a: He was worried the medicine and charger would be forgotten again, as at Nani's, and wanted them checked first.

qa.q: What else could help the family on their next trip?
qa.a: Keeping this list for next time, so they start from a tested checklist instead of memory in the dark.

qa.q: What was the list like for Gurleen?
qa.a: Gurleen was the one with a fever and no medicine last time, and now she even wants to tick the snacks herself.

grounding: During a power cut before an early start, a boy writes the items forgotten on a past trip at the top of the packing list.
